profile.address: 888, South Stadium Drive, Baton Rouge, East Baton Rouge Parish, Louisiana, 70808
profile.reading:
The Center for Computation & Technology, LSU's interdisciplinary supercomputing and digital-research institute, is housed at 888 South Stadium Drive in Baton Rouge in a building whose construction was itself a notable local development story. The three-story, roughly 94,000-square-foot Louisiana Digital Media Center was built as a joint project of LSU, the State of Louisiana, the City of Baton Rouge, the Baton Rouge Area Chamber, and video-game publisher Electronic Arts, at a reported construction cost of about $30 million. Ground was broken in July 2011, and the building was completed and occupied -- with CCT relocating into it -- in August 2013. Located near LSU's John M. Parker Coliseum, the building was designed to co-locate CCT's research operations with EA's game-development studio under one roof: EA's development team occupied one floor while CCT's research groups, including its Cultural Computing faculty cluster, occupied another, with shared classroom, auditorium, and conference space intended to connect LSU's new Digital Media Arts and Engineering degree program directly to industry.

CCT itself is best known publicly for the sequence of supercomputers it has operated for LSU and Louisiana researchers, including systems named SuperMike, SuperMike-II, Tezpur, and SuperMIC, supporting computational science across engineering, the physical sciences, and digital media research. What is not publicly documented is a technical description of the data center or machine-room space within the Digital Media Center building itself -- neither LSU nor CCT publishes power capacity, cooling architecture, or raised-floor square footage figures for the facility, and no independent reporting on those specifications was located.

That gap is consistent with the nature of the institution: CCT is a university research computing center, not a commercial or colocation data center, and its public communications focus on research output, supercomputer specifications at the system level, and academic partnerships rather than on the building's infrastructure. Readers interested in CCT's computing capacity are better served by the center's published supercomputer specifications than by facility-level detail, which LSU has not made part of its public record for this address. Louisiana's Digital Media Arts and Engineering (DMAE) program, launched alongside the building's opening, was designed to feed graduates directly into the state's growing video-game and visual-effects industry, with EA's on-site studio serving as both a working game-development office and a training ground for students moving between coursework and industry practice. State and local officials at the time framed the project explicitly as an economic-development bet: bringing a major entertainment-industry employer onto a public university campus, in the officials' own words, "for the first time," to anchor a digital-media cluster in Baton Rouge rather than losing that talent to established hubs like Los Angeles or Austin. CCT's research mission spans high-performance computing, computational science, and digital media and visual arts, reflecting the same academic-industry mix the building itself was built to support.

reading.body:
LSU's Center for Computation and Technology occupies the Louisiana Digital Media Center, a 94,000-square-foot building completed in 2013 on LSU's Baton Rouge campus. The center operates supercomputers for university research in engineering, physical sciences, and digital media, but publishes no data-center specifications: no power capacity, no cooling architecture, and no machine-room footage appear in LSU's public record for this address. Understanding CCT's infrastructure capacity requires consulting the center's published supercomputer system specifications rather than facility-level detail.

CCT was built as a joint project of LSU, the State of Louisiana, the City of Baton Rouge, and Electronic Arts, with EA's game-development studio co-located on-site to connect the university's Digital Media Arts and Engineering program directly to industry. The building was framed by state and local officials as an economic-development anchor to retain digital-media talent in Baton Rouge. The collaboration between a research computing center and a commercial game publisher under one roof was unusual for its time, but CCT itself has remained focused on publishing research output and supercomputer specifications rather than infrastructure benchmarks.

Louisiana publishes power capacity figures for only three of its four mapped data-center facilities statewide, totaling 7.7 MW across the state. This campus ranks fourth among those four and contributes no published megawatt figure to the state total. For readers tracking grid constraints on AI scaling, CCT's infrastructure capacity is not quantified in the public record.
